narrative:
The model estimated a 60.6% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, that is a somewhat higher-than-even risk estimate, and the admissions decision treated that risk as too high for approval. This is a risk estimate, not a certainty about your ability or future performance.

The denial was driven mainly by your third-year class standing. Your third-year decile was 2, well below the average of about 5.8 among accepted students, and this was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. The second most influential factor was your LSAT score. At 42, above the accepted-student average of about 37.2, it pushed toward passing and worked in your favor, but it was not enough to offset the academic-standing concerns. The third most important factor was your first-year class standing: your decile of 2 was also below the accepted average of 6.0, adding further weight toward the failure prediction. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.10 versus the accepted average of 3.23 was slightly below the accepted profile as well.

Next, contact admissions promptly to ask whether an appeal or reconsideration process exists and what additional information could support your case. Provide context for your low class rankings, such as grading curves, health or personal circumstances, and any upward trend. Ask for specific guidance on strengthening your application, and consider academic advising or a bar-readiness plan that can demonstrate your ability to succeed.
